days.title: Edge Network Services: CloudFront, Global Accelerator, and Load Balancing

concepts.heading: CloudFront Caching and Origin Behavior
concepts.body: Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network that caches content at edge locations close to end users, reducing latency for repeat requests and offloading traffic from the origin. Cache behaviors let you route different URL path patterns to different origins and apply different TTLs, and Origin Shield adds an additional caching layer in front of the origin to further reduce origin load during cache misses. Origin groups let you configure a primary and a secondary origin (such as two S3 buckets or ALBs) with automatic failover triggered by specific HTTP status codes. On the exam, remember that CloudFront's strength is caching cacheable HTTP(S) content, not accelerating dynamic or non-HTTP traffic.

concepts.heading: Global Accelerator and Anycast Acceleration
concepts.body: AWS Global Accelerator assigns two static anycast IP addresses that route traffic onto the AWS global network backbone at the nearest edge location, then carries it over AWS's private network to the application, bypassing much of the public internet. Unlike CloudFront, it supports both TCP and UDP protocols and does not cache content, making it suitable for gaming servers, VoIP, IoT, and other non-HTTP workloads. It continuously health-checks endpoint groups and can fail traffic over to a healthy region in seconds, faster than typical DNS-based failover because clients keep the same anycast IP. The static IPs are also useful for firewall allow-listing since they never change.

concepts.heading: Choosing CloudFront vs Global Accelerator
concepts.body: The primary decision criterion is whether the traffic is cacheable HTTP(S) content or not: if it is, CloudFront reduces latency and origin load through caching; if the traffic is TCP/UDP, non-HTTP, or must not be cached (real-time gaming, financial trading, VoIP), Global Accelerator is the better fit. A secondary factor is failover speed: CloudFront origin failover happens per-request at the CDN layer, while Global Accelerator can shift all traffic for a static IP to another region almost instantly via health checks. Some architectures use both together, for example CloudFront for static assets and Global Accelerator in front of an API needing low, consistent latency for non-cacheable calls.

concepts.heading: API Gateway Edge-Optimized vs Regional Endpoints
concepts.body: Edge-optimized API Gateway endpoints are automatically fronted by an AWS-managed CloudFront distribution, reducing latency for geographically distributed clients. Regional endpoints suit clients in the same Region as the API, or cases where you want your own CloudFront distribution or WAF in front for more control over caching and security rules. Private API endpoints are reachable only from within a VPC via an interface VPC endpoint and are never exposed to the internet, the correct choice for internal-only APIs. A common exam trap assumes edge-optimized is always best; if clients are regional or custom caching/WAF placement is needed, regional is usually correct.

concepts.heading: Load Balancers as Origins and Endpoints
concepts.body: Elastic Load Balancers frequently sit behind these edge services as the actual origin or endpoint: an Application Load Balancer can be a CloudFront origin for dynamic content, and both ALB and Network Load Balancer can be registered as endpoints in a Global Accelerator endpoint group. Global Accelerator can also route directly to Elastic IP addresses or EC2 instances when a full load balancer isn't required. Health checks on load balancer target groups propagate up to influence both CloudFront origin failover and Global Accelerator endpoint health, so target group health check configuration is foundational before the deeper load balancer content later this week.

examPoints: Look for keywords like real-time, UDP, gaming, VoIP, or non-cacheable dynamic traffic requiring fast global failover — these point to Global Accelerator, not CloudFront.

When a question describes multiple origins that should fail over automatically for a CloudFront distribution, the answer is an origin group with failover criteria, not multiple cache behaviors or Lambda@Edge.

quiz.q: A mobile game studio runs UDP-based game servers in two AWS Regions and needs to route players to the healthiest, lowest-latency endpoint without any content caching. Which service should they use?
choices: Amazon CloudFront with a custom cache policy
quiz.explain: Global Accelerator uses anycast IPs and continuous health checks over the AWS backbone to accelerate non-HTTP TCP/UDP traffic; CloudFront is built for cacheable HTTP(S) content and would not help here.

quiz.q: A company wants its CloudFront distribution to automatically serve content from a backup S3 bucket in another Region whenever the primary bucket returns 5xx errors. What should they configure?
choices: Two separate cache behaviors for the same path
An origin group with failover criteria based on HTTP status codes
A Lambda@Edge function that retries requests
Field-level encryption on the primary origin
quiz.explain: Origin groups let CloudFront automatically fail over from a primary to a secondary origin when specific status codes are returned; cache behaviors route by path pattern and do not provide failover.

days.recap: CloudFront accelerates cacheable HTTP(S) content through edge caching and origin groups, while Global Accelerator uses anycast IPs to speed up any TCP/UDP traffic with fast health-check-based failover, and the same cacheable-vs-not logic decides between edge-optimized and regional API Gateway endpoints.

days.title: DNS Solution Design: Public, Private, and Hybrid Resolution

concepts.heading: Public Hosted Zones and Domain Registration
concepts.body: A public hosted zone in Route 53 holds DNS records resolvable from anywhere on the internet, typically paired with a registered domain whose authoritative name servers point at the hosted zone. Record types include standard A, AAAA, CNAME, and MX records plus the Route 53-specific Alias record, which lets you point a zone apex or any record at AWS resources such as CloudFront, ALB, or S3 without the extra lookup and cost of a CNAME. Designing public zones well includes planning TTLs for how quickly changes propagate and using routing policies to influence which answer a resolver receives.

concepts.heading: Private Hosted Zones and Multi-VPC Association
concepts.body: A private hosted zone answers DNS queries only from VPCs it is explicitly associated with, allowing internal service names to resolve inside your network without being exposed publicly. A single private hosted zone can be associated with multiple VPCs, including VPCs in different AWS accounts through an authorization and association handshake, letting a central network account own a namespace that many application VPCs reuse. Because a private zone can override the same domain name that exists publicly, be careful about split-horizon DNS scenarios where internal clients should get different (typically private) answers than external clients for the same domain.

concepts.heading: Route 53 Resolver for Hybrid DNS
concepts.body: Route 53 Resolver provides two endpoint types that let DNS resolution flow between AWS and on-premises networks: inbound endpoints let on-premises DNS servers forward queries into AWS to resolve private hosted zone or VPC records, and outbound endpoints let VPC resources forward queries for on-premises domains out to on-premises DNS servers. Both endpoint types are backed by elastic network interfaces placed in your VPC subnets and should span multiple Availability Zones for resiliency. This bidirectional design is the standard way to achieve a unified hybrid DNS namespace without running your own DNS forwarders on EC2.

concepts.heading: Route 53 Health Checks and DNS Failover
concepts.body: Route 53 health checks continuously probe an endpoint (an IP, a domain, or a CloudWatch alarm) and mark it healthy or unhealthy, which failover routing policy uses to automatically stop returning an unhealthy resource's IP address. Health checks can also aggregate the status of child health checks (calculated health checks) to model more complex availability logic, such as requiring a minimum number of healthy resources across a fleet. Because clients and resolvers cache answers according to TTL, failover speed is bounded by TTL, which is why low TTLs are paired with health-check-based failover for faster recovery.

concepts.heading: Routing Policies for Traffic Management
concepts.body: Beyond simple routing, Route 53 supports weighted (percentage-based distribution, useful for canary releases), latency-based (route to the Region with lowest measured latency), geolocation (route based on the querier's location for compliance or localization), and geoproximity with bias (shift traffic geographically) routing policies. Multivalue answer routing returns several healthy IP addresses to add basic client-side load distribution and health-check awareness without a full load balancer. Combining these policies, for example weighted routing nested inside a latency-based policy for canary releases, is done using Traffic Flow, which lets you visually design and version complex resolution logic as a single traffic policy record.

examPoints: When a scenario needs on-premises DNS servers and AWS Route 53 to resolve each other's names in both directions, the answer is Route 53 Resolver with both an inbound and an outbound endpoint, not a single endpoint or a manually managed DNS forwarder.

When multiple VPCs, possibly across accounts, need to share the same internal service names, look for private hosted zone association to multiple VPCs rather than duplicating records in separate zones.

quiz.q: A company needs on-premises DNS servers to resolve names in an AWS private hosted zone, and also needs EC2 instances in the VPC to resolve names hosted by the on-premises DNS servers. What should they deploy?
choices: Only a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint
A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint and an outbound endpoint with forwarding rules
A public hosted zone shared with on-premises
A single EC2 instance running BIND
quiz.explain: The inbound endpoint handles on-premises-to-AWS queries and the outbound endpoint with forwarding rules handles AWS-to-on-premises queries; using only one endpoint leaves one direction unresolved.

quiz.q: Several VPCs across three different AWS accounts need to resolve the same internal service names consistently. What is the most operationally efficient design?
choices: Create a separate private hosted zone per VPC with identical records
Create one private hosted zone and associate it with all the VPCs across accounts
Hardcode IP addresses in each application
quiz.explain: A private hosted zone can be associated with multiple VPCs, including across accounts via authorization, avoiding duplicated records and configuration drift.

days.recap: Public hosted zones serve internet-wide resolution while private hosted zones can be shared across many VPCs and accounts, Route 53 Resolver's inbound and outbound endpoints stitch together on-premises and AWS DNS, and health checks combined with routing policies give you failover and traffic management.

days.title: Load Balancer Design: Choosing ALB, NLB, and Gateway Load Balancer

concepts.heading: Application Load Balancer for Layer 7 Routing
concepts.body: The Application Load Balancer operates at Layer 7 and can make routing decisions based on HTTP/HTTPS attributes such as host header, URL path, HTTP method, query string, and headers, making it the natural fit for microservices and container-based applications needing path- or host-based routing. It integrates directly with AWS WAF for layer 7 protections and supports sticky sessions, redirect and fixed-response actions, and authentication actions (Cognito or OIDC) at the load balancer itself. ALB targets can be EC2 instances, IP addresses (including on-premises via Direct Connect/VPN), Lambda functions, or another ALB, which is unique among the load balancer types.

concepts.heading: Network Load Balancer for Extreme Performance
concepts.body: The Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4, handling TCP, UDP, and TLS traffic with extremely low latency and the ability to handle millions of requests per second while preserving the client source IP by default. NLB supports static IP addresses per Availability Zone (or Elastic IPs you assign), important when downstream firewalls need a stable, whitelistable IP, and it is the only load balancer type usable as a target behind a Gateway Load Balancer or referenced by a PrivateLink endpoint service. For TLS traffic, NLB can either terminate TLS or pass encrypted traffic through untouched when end-to-end encryption is a compliance requirement.

concepts.heading: Gateway Load Balancer for Transparent Traffic Inspection
concepts.body: Gateway Load Balancer operates at Layer 3/4 and is purpose-built to distribute traffic transparently to a fleet of third-party virtual appliances, such as firewalls or IDS/IPS tools, without altering the packet's source or destination. It uses the GENEVE protocol (port 6081) to encapsulate traffic between the GWLB endpoint in a consumer VPC and the GWLB itself, which fronts the appliance fleet, enabling a centralized inspection VPC pattern where traffic between VPCs, or leaving to the internet, is inspected before continuing. GWLB Endpoints are the consumer-side construct inserted into route tables to redirect traffic to the appliance transparently.

concepts.heading: TLS Termination Strategy and Certificate Placement
concepts.body: Deciding where to terminate TLS is a recurring decision: terminating at the ALB or NLB simplifies certificate management and offloads CPU-intensive TLS negotiation from backend instances, while re-encrypting to the backend or passing through end-to-end satisfies stricter compliance frameworks that prohibit any plaintext transmission inside the VPC. AWS Certificate Manager integrates with ALB, NLB, and CloudFront to issue and automatically renew public TLS certificates at no additional cost. For mutual TLS or internal service-to-service certificates, ACM Private CA issues certificates from a private certificate authority you control, covered in more depth in the security domain.

concepts.heading: Load Balancer Integration with Containers and Kubernetes
concepts.body: For containerized workloads on Amazon EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller watches Kubernetes Ingress and Service resources and automatically provisions and configures ALBs (for Ingress) or NLBs (for Service type LoadBalancer), keeping target group membership in sync as pods scale up and down. This avoids manually managing load balancers outside of Kubernetes and ensures target health checks track actual pod readiness. Understanding that ALB generally fits HTTP-based Ingress while NLB fits non-HTTP or extreme-performance Kubernetes services helps map EKS networking scenarios to the correct load balancer type.

examPoints: A requirement to transparently inspect all VPC traffic through third-party firewall or IDS/IPS appliances without changing traffic flow is the signature scenario for Gateway Load Balancer using GENEVE encapsulation.
When a scenario demands end-to-end encryption all the way to the backend for compliance, look for NLB with TLS passthrough or backend re-encryption rather than TLS termination at the load balancer.

quiz.q: A security team needs all traffic entering and leaving multiple VPCs to be transparently inspected by a fleet of third-party firewall appliances, without modifying the original packet headers. Which load balancer should front the appliance fleet?
choices: Network Load Balancer with TLS termination
quiz.explain: Gateway Load Balancer is purpose-built for transparent, in-line traffic inspection using GENEVE encapsulation, preserving original packet headers; ALB and standard NLB are not designed for this appliance-insertion pattern.

quiz.q: An application must maintain end-to-end TLS encryption from the client all the way to the backend instance with no intermediate decryption, due to a compliance mandate. What load balancer configuration satisfies this?
choices: ALB with TLS termination and HTTP to the backend
CloudFront only, with no load balancer
quiz.explain: NLB TLS passthrough forwards encrypted TCP traffic to the backend without decrypting it at the load balancer, satisfying strict end-to-end encryption requirements.

days.recap: ALB handles Layer 7 content-based routing with native WAF and container integration, NLB delivers Layer 4 extreme performance with static IPs and optional TLS passthrough, and Gateway Load Balancer transparently inserts third-party inspection appliances into the traffic path using GENEVE, with ACM handling certificate issuance across the board.

days.title: Designing Hybrid Network Logging and Monitoring

concepts.heading: Defining Monitoring Requirements Up Front
concepts.body: Effective network monitoring design starts by explicitly defining what needs to be observed (traffic volume, latency, packet loss, error/reject rates), where it needs to be collected (VPC, Direct Connect, VPN, Transit Gateway, on-premises links), and how quickly issues must be detected. Skipping this step commonly leads to either an overwhelming volume of unused logs or blind spots at exactly the layer where a future incident occurs, such as missing Transit Gateway attachment-level metrics while only capturing VPC Flow Logs. The exam frequently tests whether you can match a stated requirement to the correct log or metric source rather than a generic 'turn on logging' answer.

concepts.heading: VPC Flow Logs for Traffic Visibility
concepts.body: VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about IP traffic at the VPC, subnet, or elastic network interface level, recording source/destination IP and port, protocol, packet and byte counts, and whether traffic was accepted or rejected, and can be delivered to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Amazon Data Firehose. They are invaluable for auditing which traffic is blocked by security groups or NACLs and for capacity or cost analysis, but they do not capture packet payloads, so they cannot be used for deep packet inspection. Custom log formats let you select only the fields you need, reducing storage costs versus the full default field set.

concepts.heading: Transit Gateway Network Manager for Global Topology
concepts.body: AWS Transit Gateway Network Manager provides a single visual map of your global network, including Transit Gateways, VPC and VPN attachments, Direct Connect connections, and even on-premises SD-WAN devices registered through supported third-party integrations. It surfaces both topology and events (route changes, link state changes, attachment status), and publishes CloudWatch metrics for bytes in/out and packet drop counts per attachment. This is the go-to tool whenever a scenario requires visibility across a hybrid, multi-Region network as a whole, rather than a single VPC's internal traffic.

concepts.heading: VPC Reachability Analyzer for Static Path Validation
concepts.body: Reachability Analyzer performs a point-in-time static analysis of your network configuration, evaluating route tables, security groups, network ACLs, and other config to determine whether a packet from a specified source could reach a specified destination, without ever sending an actual packet. When it finds the path is blocked, it identifies the exact component and rule responsible, drastically shortening root-cause analysis versus manually tracing route tables and security group rules by hand. Because it's configuration-based, it can also be used proactively before deploying a change, and it supports cross-account and cross-Region analysis when resources are shared appropriately.

concepts.heading: Alerting and Automated Response with CloudWatch
concepts.body: CloudWatch alarms set thresholds on metrics gathered from Flow Logs, Network Manager, VPN tunnel status, or Direct Connect connection state, and can trigger SNS notifications or Lambda-based automated remediation, such as failing over to a backup path when a VPN tunnel goes down. CloudWatch Logs Insights allows ad hoc querying across Flow Logs to quickly answer questions like which source IPs generated the most rejected traffic recently. Designing dashboards that combine Network Manager topology health with CloudWatch alarm state gives operators a single pane of glass for hybrid network health.

examPoints: When a question asks to validate whether two resources can communicate without generating live traffic, the keyword 'without sending actual packets' or 'static analysis' points directly to VPC Reachability Analyzer.

When the scope is the entire hybrid network including Direct Connect, VPN, Transit Gateway, and on-premises SD-WAN devices visualized as one map, the answer is Transit Gateway Network Manager, not VPC Flow Logs.

quiz.q: A network engineer wants to confirm that a planned security group change will not break connectivity between two EC2 instances, before applying it in production, and without generating real traffic. What tool should they use?
quiz.explain: Reachability Analyzer statically evaluates configuration to predict connectivity without sending packets; Flow Logs only show traffic that has actually occurred.

quiz.q: An organization wants a single visual map of its Transit Gateways, Direct Connect connections, VPN attachments, and on-premises SD-WAN appliances across multiple Regions. What should they use?
quiz.explain: Network Manager is specifically designed to visualize and monitor a global, hybrid network topology across Regions and on-premises links.

days.recap: Good hybrid monitoring design starts with explicit requirements, uses VPC Flow Logs for traffic metadata, Transit Gateway Network Manager for global topology and events, and Reachability Analyzer for pre-emptive static path validation, tying together into CloudWatch alarms for alerting and automated response.

days.title: On-Premises to AWS Routing Design: BGP and Redundancy Models

concepts.heading: BGP Fundamentals for Hybrid Connections
concepts.body: Both Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN use BGP as their dynamic routing protocol, exchanging routes between your on-premises Autonomous System and AWS. Each side advertises prefixes along with path attributes, and AWS assigns its side an ASN while you configure your own customer-side ASN. Understanding the three core path attributes, AS Path, Local Preference, and MED, is essential because virtually every route-preference scenario on the exam maps back to one of them, and static routing is only viable for simple, single-path connections without automatic failover.

concepts.heading: Controlling Route Preference with BGP Attributes
concepts.body: AS Path Prepending artificially lengthens the advertised AS Path to make a route less preferred by the remote side, commonly used to make one connection a backup by prepending your ASN multiple times on that path's advertisement. Local Preference is set locally and influences outbound traffic, i.e., which path your own network prefers to send traffic out on, and is not advertised externally. MED is advertised to a peer to suggest which of your multiple entry points that peer should prefer for traffic destined to you, effectively influencing inbound traffic, though the receiving side can choose to ignore it.

concepts.heading: Active-Active vs Active-Passive Redundancy Models
concepts.body: In an active-active design, both connections carry production traffic simultaneously, maximizing usable bandwidth and providing automatic, often sub-second BGP-driven failover if one path fails, at the cost of more complex route-preference tuning. In an active-passive design, BGP attributes are deliberately configured so all traffic prefers one connection, with the second sitting idle except during a failure, which is simpler to reason about but wastes backup capacity during normal operation. The choice usually comes down to whether the requirement emphasizes aggregate throughput or operational simplicity.

concepts.heading: Direct Connect Resiliency Best Practices
concepts.body: AWS explicitly recommends provisioning multiple Direct Connect connections at physically separate Direct Connect locations (different buildings, ideally different providers) to eliminate a single point of failure at the facility, cross-connect, or device level; two connections terminating in the same location or device rack still share fate on a facility-level outage. AWS publishes named resiliency models describing specific combinations of locations and devices to meet different SLA targets, and exam scenarios asking for 'the highest resiliency' typically require diverse locations and diverse devices, not just diverse connections.

concepts.heading: Combining Direct Connect and VPN for Backup
concepts.body: A very common hybrid pattern uses Direct Connect as the primary high-bandwidth, low-latency path and a Site-to-Site VPN over the internet as an automatic backup, with BGP attributes tuned so Direct Connect is preferred under normal conditions. This can be implemented either as a VPN terminating independently on a Virtual Private Gateway/Transit Gateway, or as VPN riding over the Direct Connect public/transit VIF for encryption without depending on the public internet. Recovery time in this pattern is governed by BGP hold timers and, if configured, Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD), which detects link failure far faster than default BGP timers alone.

examPoints: A scenario describing two Direct Connect connections where one should only carry traffic if the other fails, based on the traffic AWS sends back to you, points to Local Preference influencing outbound traffic from AWS's perspective — read carefully which side is being controlled.

'Highest possible resiliency' or 'eliminate single points of failure' for Direct Connect nearly always means connections at separate Direct Connect locations and separate devices, not simply two connections at the same location.

quiz.q: A company wants outbound traffic from its VPC to always prefer Direct Connect over a backup VPN connection whenever Direct Connect is available. Which BGP attribute should be configured to influence this outbound path selection?
choices: AS Path Prepending on the VPN side only
Community strings with no local effect
quiz.explain: Local Preference directly controls which path a router prefers for its own outbound traffic; MED instead influences what a neighboring AS prefers for traffic coming toward you.

quiz.q: For maximum Direct Connect resiliency, eliminating both facility and device-level single points of failure, what should a company provision?
choices: Two connections at the same Direct Connect location and same router
Two connections at physically separate Direct Connect locations on separate devices
A single high-bandwidth Direct Connect connection
A single VPN connection instead of Direct Connect
quiz.explain: AWS's maximum resiliency model requires diverse locations and diverse devices; connections sharing a location or device still share a common failure domain.

days.recap: Direct Connect and VPN both rely on BGP, where Local Preference controls your outbound path choice, MED suggests inbound path preference to a peer, and AS Path Prepending discourages a path altogether, all combining with active-active or active-passive redundancy models and geographically diverse Direct Connect locations to build resilient hybrid connectivity.

days.title: SD-WAN Integration and Advanced Direct Connect Features

concepts.heading: Direct Connect Gateway for Multi-Region, Multi-VPC Access
concepts.body: Direct Connect Gateway is a globally available construct that lets a single Direct Connect connection (via a private or transit virtual interface) reach multiple VPCs or Transit Gateways across different AWS Regions, without a separate physical connection per Region. This is the standard solution for a global organization with a single on-premises data center that needs private connectivity into VPCs spread across multiple Regions. A key limitation to remember is that a Direct Connect Gateway associated to a Transit Gateway can only be associated with one Transit Gateway per Region, though it can connect to Transit Gateways in multiple different Regions.

concepts.heading: Transit Gateway Connect for SD-WAN Attachments
concepts.body: Transit Gateway Connect provides a way to attach SD-WAN appliances (or other virtual/physical routing appliances) to a Transit Gateway using GRE tunneling combined with BGP for dynamic routing, supporting significantly higher aggregate bandwidth per attachment than a standard site-to-site VPN attachment. This makes it the preferred integration point when an organization already runs an SD-WAN fabric at its branch offices and wants AWS Transit Gateway to become just another node in that fabric. A Connect attachment itself rides on top of an existing VPC or Direct Connect (via transit VIF) attachment to the Transit Gateway.

concepts.heading: SD-WAN Fabric Integration Architecture
concepts.body: In a typical SD-WAN integration, each branch office's SD-WAN appliance establishes a Connect peer (a GRE tunnel with BGP) to the Transit Gateway Connect attachment, effectively extending the branch's SD-WAN overlay into AWS as if the Transit Gateway were another SD-WAN edge device. This allows centralized, policy-based routing decisions made by the SD-WAN controller to apply consistently across branch-to-branch and branch-to-cloud traffic. Because Connect attachments can have multiple Connect peers, a single attachment can aggregate connectivity from several SD-WAN appliances or provide additional bandwidth by load-balancing across peers.

concepts.heading: Overcoming VPN Bandwidth Limits
concepts.body: A standard Site-to-Site VPN tunnel is capped at roughly 1.25 Gbps of throughput per tunnel, so achieving higher aggregate bandwidth traditionally required Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing across several VPN connections and tunnels, adding operational complexity in matching routes and monitoring multiple tunnels. Transit Gateway Connect bypasses this per-tunnel ceiling by supporting much higher throughput on a single GRE-based Connect peer, making it the more scalable choice when a growing SD-WAN or appliance-based deployment starts to outgrow what VPN/ECMP can practically deliver.

examPoints: A requirement for one Direct Connect connection to reach VPCs or Transit Gateways in multiple AWS Regions is the classic signal for Direct Connect Gateway.

When an SD-WAN appliance needs to attach directly to a Transit Gateway with more bandwidth than a standard VPN tunnel provides, the answer is Transit Gateway Connect using GRE and BGP, not additional VPN tunnels.

quiz.q: A global enterprise has one on-premises data center connected via a single Direct Connect connection and needs private access to VPCs in three different AWS Regions. What should they deploy?
choices: A separate Direct Connect connection per Region
A Direct Connect Gateway associated with VPCs/Transit Gateways in each Region
Site-to-Site VPN in addition to Direct Connect for each Region
quiz.explain: Direct Connect Gateway lets a single connection reach VPCs or Transit Gateways across multiple Regions; building a separate physical connection per Region would be unnecessarily costly and complex.

quiz.q: An organization's branch offices use an SD-WAN fabric and want to attach their SD-WAN appliances directly to a Transit Gateway with more bandwidth than a single VPN tunnel allows. What should they use?
choices: Additional standard Site-to-Site VPN tunnels only
Transit Gateway Connect with GRE and BGP
quiz.explain: Transit Gateway Connect is purpose-built for attaching SD-WAN or routing appliances via GRE/BGP with higher throughput than the per-tunnel VPN limit.

days.recap: Direct Connect Gateway extends a single connection's reach across Regions to multiple VPCs and Transit Gateways, while Transit Gateway Connect uses GRE and BGP to bring SD-WAN appliances directly onto the Transit Gateway with far higher bandwidth than standard VPN tunnels, which otherwise require ECMP across multiple tunnels to scale.

days.title: Multi-Account, Multi-Region VPC Connectivity Strategy

concepts.heading: Comparing VPC Connectivity Options
concepts.body: VPC Peering provides a simple, non-transitive one-to-one connection between two VPCs with no additional hourly cost, but does not scale well past a handful of VPCs since every pair needs its own peering connection with no hub for centralized routing or inspection. Transit Gateway acts as a fully managed, transitive hub-and-spoke router scaling to thousands of attachments with centralized route table control, at the cost of a per-attachment and per-GB processing charge. AWS PrivateLink exposes a specific service, not full network reachability, privately across VPCs or accounts via interface endpoints. VPC Sharing, built on AWS RAM, lets a central account share subnets from a single VPC to other accounts, letting them launch resources directly into shared subnets.

concepts.heading: Handling Overlapping CIDR Blocks
concepts.body: When two VPCs need to be connected but share overlapping or identical private IP ranges, common after a merger or acquisition, VPC Peering and Transit Gateway attachments cannot be used because both rely on IP-based routing that becomes ambiguous with duplicate address space. AWS PrivateLink sidesteps this entirely because the consumer VPC only sees the endpoint's private IP in its own address space and never routes directly into the provider VPC's CIDR, making it the standard answer whenever overlapping CIDRs must be connected at the service level. When full network-level connectivity across overlapping CIDRs is unavoidable, the alternative is a more complex NAT-based translation layer.

concepts.heading: VPC Sharing for Centralized Network Ownership
concepts.body: VPC Sharing lets a central 'network' account own the VPC and its subnets while sharing individual subnets, via AWS RAM, to other 'application' owner accounts, who can then launch EC2 instances, RDS databases, and other resources directly into the shared subnet. Billing and resource ownership remain with the account that creates the resource, but the underlying VPC, subnet, and core networking configuration stay centrally managed, reducing the proliferation of VPCs across a large organization. A key constraint is that participant accounts cannot modify shared subnet properties or route tables, and certain resource types have restrictions in shared subnets.

concepts.heading: A Framework for Choosing the Right Connectivity Option
concepts.body: When facing a connectivity design question, work through: how many VPCs need to connect (a handful favors Peering, many favors Transit Gateway); whether transitive routing is required (Peering cannot provide it, Transit Gateway can); whether only a specific service needs exposure versus full network reachability (favoring PrivateLink); and whether CIDR ranges overlap (favoring PrivateLink). Applying this framework quickly eliminates two or three of the four options in most exam scenarios, leaving the correct answer clearly identifiable.

concepts.heading: Combining Connectivity Options in Real Architectures
concepts.body: Large organizations frequently combine these tools: Transit Gateway as the backbone for VPC-to-VPC and hybrid connectivity, VPC Sharing to reduce the number of VPCs application teams manage day to day, and PrivateLink to expose specific shared services without granting broader network access even to VPCs that are already Transit Gateway spokes. Recognizing that these tools solve different layers of the problem, network-level versus service-level access, is a recurring theme across multiple exam domains.

examPoints: Overlapping or duplicate private IP address ranges between two VPCs that must be connected at the service level is the clearest signal to choose AWS PrivateLink, since it does not require unique, routable CIDRs.

A requirement for a central networking team to own and manage a VPC's core configuration while other teams' accounts launch resources into it, with separate billing per account, describes VPC Sharing via AWS RAM.

quiz.q: Following a company acquisition, two VPCs with identical private IP CIDR blocks need to connect so that consumers in one VPC can reach a specific internal API hosted in the other. What should they use?
choices: AWS PrivateLink using an interface VPC endpoint
Transit Gateway with a single route table
Manually renumbering is required before any connection is possible
quiz.explain: PrivateLink exposes the service through an endpoint using the consumer's own address space, working correctly even with overlapping CIDRs, unlike Peering or Transit Gateway.

quiz.q: A central networking team wants to own and manage a VPC's subnets and route tables while several application teams, each with separate AWS accounts and billing, launch resources directly into that VPC. Which approach fits best?
choices: Create a separate VPC per application account
Share subnets from the central VPC using AWS RAM (VPC Sharing)
Use PrivateLink for all resource types
Use VPC Peering between each application account and the central account
quiz.explain: VPC Sharing lets a central account own and manage the VPC while other accounts launch and pay for their own resources within shared subnets.

days.recap: Choosing among VPC Peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink, and VPC Sharing comes down to connection scale, transitivity, whether service-level or full network access is needed, and whether CIDR ranges overlap, with PrivateLink as the go-to for overlapping IP space and VPC Sharing for centralized subnet ownership across accounts.

days.title: Domain 1 Review: Network Design

concepts.heading: Edge, DNS, and Load Balancing as One Traffic-Entry Story
concepts.body: Step back and see Days 1 through 3 as a single narrative about how traffic first enters your architecture: Route 53 decides which IP a client resolves to, CloudFront or Global Accelerator decides how that traffic is accelerated and where it enters the AWS network, and ALB, NLB, or GWLB decides how it's distributed and inspected once it arrives. Exam scenarios often chain these together, so practice narrating a full request path end to end rather than studying each service in isolation.

concepts.heading: Hybrid Connectivity as a Second Storyline
concepts.body: Days 4 through 6 build the hybrid connectivity storyline: BGP and its attributes govern route preference across Direct Connect and VPN, Direct Connect Gateway and Transit Gateway Connect extend that connectivity across Regions and into SD-WAN fabrics, and Network Manager plus Reachability Analyzer give you visibility and validation over the whole thing. When reviewing, be able to explain why a design would choose Direct Connect Gateway over multiple point-to-point connections, and why Local Preference versus MED matters for which direction of traffic you're controlling.

concepts.heading: The Multi-VPC Connectivity Decision Framework
concepts.body: Day 7's framework, connection count, transitivity, service-level versus network-level access, and CIDR overlap, is one of the most heavily tested decision trees on the exam because it recurs any time a scenario says 'multiple VPCs' or 'multiple accounts.' Drill yourself by writing four one-line justifications: when Peering wins, when Transit Gateway wins, when PrivateLink wins, and when VPC Sharing wins, until you can answer instantly without re-deriving the logic from scratch.

concepts.heading: Design Domain Exam Strategy
concepts.body: Network Design carries the largest single-domain weight on the exam at 30%, so investing extra review time here pays off disproportionately; prioritize scenario-style practice questions that combine two or more services from this week since standalone single-service questions are comparatively rare. Keep a running list of any service pair you found yourself confusing this week and revisit that list specifically before the exam.

examPoints: Whenever a scenario mixes two or more services from this week (for example DNS + load balancing + edge acceleration), identify each service's job separately before choosing an overall answer, rather than looking for one service that does everything.
For any 'connect multiple VPCs/accounts' scenario, run through connection count, transitivity, service vs. network level, and CIDR overlap in that order before selecting an answer.

quiz.q: A design requires global users to be routed to the lowest-latency healthy Region, with automatic failover if a Region's health check fails, for standard HTTPS web traffic. Which combination best fits?
choices: Global Accelerator only, no DNS involved
Route 53 latency-based or failover routing combined with health checks, plus CloudFront for caching
A single static A record with no health checks
quiz.explain: For cacheable HTTPS content, Route 53 routing policies with health checks handle Region selection and failover, and CloudFront adds edge caching; Global Accelerator would be reserved for non-cacheable or non-HTTP needs.

quiz.q: Two VPCs belonging to recently merged companies have overlapping CIDR blocks and need to connect at the service level only. What is the correct choice, based on this week's material?
choices: Re-architect one VPC's CIDR before connecting
quiz.explain: PrivateLink is unaffected by overlapping CIDRs because it operates at the service level within the consumer's own address space, unlike Peering or Transit Gateway.

days.recap: Domain 1 review ties together traffic entry (DNS, edge acceleration, load balancing), hybrid connectivity (BGP, Direct Connect Gateway, TGW Connect, monitoring), and the multi-VPC decision framework (Peering vs Transit Gateway vs PrivateLink vs VPC Sharing) into the complete network design picture worth 30% of the exam.

days.title: Implementing Hybrid Connectivity: Virtual Interfaces, BGP, and Verification

concepts.heading: Choosing and Configuring the Right Virtual Interface Type
concepts.body: A private virtual interface (VIF) connects Direct Connect directly to resources inside a single VPC via a Virtual Private Gateway, a public VIF gives access to AWS public service endpoints and other Regions' public IP space over Direct Connect, and a transit VIF is required whenever the Direct Connect connection needs to reach a Transit Gateway rather than a Virtual Private Gateway directly. Implementation starts with selecting the correct VIF type for the target architecture; using a private VIF where a transit VIF is needed is a common configuration mistake that prevents the intended connectivity from ever working, even though BGP itself may establish successfully.

concepts.heading: Establishing and Verifying BGP Sessions
concepts.body: After the VIF and physical/logical connection are in place, BGP is configured on both the AWS side (largely automatic) and the customer router, and the first implementation checkpoint is confirming the BGP session reaches the Established state rather than staying in Idle, Connect, or Active states, which indicate a lower-layer or configuration problem. Once established, verify that the expected routes appear in both the 'routes advertised to AWS' and 'routes received from AWS' views, since a session can be Established while still advertising the wrong prefixes due to route filters or route maps.

concepts.heading: VPN Tunnel Implementation Details
concepts.body: Implementing a Site-to-Site VPN involves selecting IKE version (IKEv2 is generally preferred for better performance and security), configuring Dead Peer Detection (DPD) timeouts to detect a failed peer and tear down a stale tunnel, and choosing between static routing (simpler, for a single fixed set of on-premises prefixes) and BGP dynamic routing (required for automatic failover and prefix changes). Each VPN connection provisions two tunnels for redundancy, and for higher aggregate throughput, multiple VPN connections combined with ECMP routing on the customer gateway can be used, provided BGP is used.

concepts.heading: Post-Implementation Connectivity Testing
concepts.body: After configuration, functional verification should include traceroute or similar path-tracing tools to confirm traffic takes the expected path and fails over correctly when a primary path is disabled, along with throughput testing to confirm the connection performs at its provisioned bandwidth. VPC Reachability Analyzer complements live traffic testing by statically confirming that the AWS-side configuration does not itself block the intended path, which is especially useful for catching security group or NACL misconfigurations.

concepts.heading: Common Implementation Pitfalls
concepts.body: Frequent hybrid connectivity implementation issues include mismatched BGP ASNs between the customer router configuration and what was specified when creating the AWS-side virtual interface, MTU mismatches (Direct Connect supports jumbo frames up to 9001 bytes on private/transit VIFs, but public VIFs and VPN are limited to 1500), and forgetting to update route tables to point traffic toward the new attachment even though the BGP session is healthy. Systematically checking VIF type, BGP session state and routes, MTU settings, and route table associations in that order resolves most 'connection is up but traffic doesn't flow' tickets.

examPoints: Any scenario requiring a Direct Connect connection to reach a Transit Gateway (rather than a single VPC's Virtual Private Gateway) requires a transit virtual interface, a frequently tested distinction from a private VIF.

After implementation, verifying BGP session state as Established and confirming the specific advertised/received routes match expectations is the standard first verification step, distinct from just checking the physical connection is up.

quiz.q: A network engineer needs to connect an existing Direct Connect connection to a Transit Gateway so it can reach multiple VPC attachments. Which virtual interface type must be used?
quiz.explain: A transit VIF is specifically required to connect Direct Connect to a Transit Gateway; a private VIF connects only to a single VPC's Virtual Private Gateway.

quiz.q: After configuring a new Direct Connect BGP session, the engineer wants to confirm implementation succeeded before troubleshooting application traffic. What should they check first?
choices: BGP session state (Established) and the specific advertised/received routes
quiz.explain: Confirming BGP reaches Established state with the correct advertised and received routes is the standard first verification step for hybrid connectivity, before layer-7 application troubleshooting.

days.recap: Implementing hybrid connectivity means choosing the correct VIF type (private, public, or transit) for the target, verifying BGP reaches Established with the expected routes, carefully configuring VPN tunnel options, and systematically checking VIF type, BGP state, MTU, and route tables when traffic doesn't flow as expected.

days.title: Implementing Multi-VPC Connectivity and Segmentation

concepts.heading: DHCP Option Sets for Consistent Name Resolution
concepts.body: When multiple VPCs are connected into a shared network, a DHCP option set defines what DNS servers, domain name, and NTP servers instances receive automatically, and in hybrid environments this is often customized to point instances at on-premises or Route 53 Resolver DNS servers rather than the default AmazonProvidedDNS. DHCP option sets are immutable once created (you must create a new set and associate it with the VPC to make a change) and apply at the VPC level, and instances need to renew their DHCP lease or be restarted to pick up a newly associated option set.

concepts.heading: Implementing Hub-and-Spoke with Transit Gateway
concepts.body: Implementing a hub-and-spoke topology means attaching each VPC to the Transit Gateway as a spoke and associating each attachment with one or more Transit Gateway route tables that control which other attachments it can reach, rather than relying on a single flat route table that would allow every spoke to reach every other spoke by default. This requires explicitly creating and associating multiple route tables and configuring route propagation carefully, since propagation and association are two distinct steps that are frequently confused during implementation.

concepts.heading: Enforcing Segmentation with Multiple Route Tables
concepts.body: To implement a requirement like 'production spoke VPCs must not talk to each other but must reach a shared services VPC', you create a production route table associated with only the production attachments (with routes only to shared services), and a separate shared-services route table with broader reachability, then associate each attachment to the appropriate table. This route-table-per-segment pattern is the core implementation mechanism for network segmentation on Transit Gateway and is tested heavily because it requires careful, explicit configuration to get right.

concepts.heading: Implementing Centralized Inspection with Network Firewall
concepts.body: The inspection VPC pattern is implemented by deploying AWS Network Firewall endpoints in a dedicated VPC, then configuring Transit Gateway and VPC route tables so that traffic between spokes, or from spokes to the internet, is routed through the inspection VPC's firewall endpoints before continuing to its destination, rather than going directly spoke-to-spoke or spoke-to-internet. This typically requires careful route table design in both the spoke VPCs and the inspection VPC, and is a common source of asymmetric routing bugs if not implemented symmetrically for both directions of traffic.

concepts.heading: Monitoring Connectivity After Implementation
concepts.body: Transit Gateway Flow Logs record traffic traversing the Transit Gateway itself, complementing VPC-level Flow Logs by showing cross-attachment traffic patterns, and per-attachment CloudWatch metrics reveal whether a specific spoke's attachment is healthy and correctly passing expected traffic volume after a segmentation change. Reviewing these metrics immediately after implementing new route tables or firewall routing is the fastest way to confirm the segmentation behaves as designed.

examPoints: A requirement that production spoke VPCs cannot reach each other but can all reach a shared services VPC is implemented with multiple Transit Gateway route tables, one per segment, not a single shared route table with security group rules alone.

Forcing all inter-VPC or outbound internet traffic through a central firewall is implemented via the inspection VPC pattern, requiring explicit route table changes in both the spoke and inspection VPCs, not just deploying the firewall appliance.

quiz.q: A company has five production spoke VPCs attached to a Transit Gateway. They must not be able to communicate with each other, but each must reach a central shared-services VPC. How should this be implemented?
choices: A single Transit Gateway route table shared by all attachments
Separate Transit Gateway route tables: one for production spokes with no spoke-to-spoke routes, one for shared services
Security groups alone, with a single flat route table
VPC Peering between each pair of production VPCs
quiz.explain: Multiple Transit Gateway route tables let you control exactly which attachments can route to which others; a single flat table would allow unwanted spoke-to-spoke communication by default.

quiz.q: An organization wants all traffic leaving its spoke VPCs for the internet to pass through a centralized AWS Network Firewall before continuing. What implementation pattern achieves this?
choices: Deploy Network Firewall in each spoke VPC independently with no route changes
The inspection VPC pattern, routing spoke traffic through a dedicated firewall VPC via Transit Gateway
Security groups configured to deny all outbound traffic
NAT Gateway alone, without a firewall
quiz.explain: The inspection VPC pattern centralizes Network Firewall in a dedicated VPC and requires explicit route table changes in spokes to direct traffic there before it continues.

days.recap: Implementing multi-VPC connectivity means consistent DHCP-provided DNS, hub-and-spoke Transit Gateway attachments governed by multiple purpose-built route tables for segmentation, the inspection VPC pattern with carefully symmetric routing for centralized firewalling, and Transit Gateway Flow Logs plus per-attachment metrics to confirm it all behaves as designed.

days.title: Implementing AWS Network Firewall

concepts.heading: Network Firewall Endpoint Architecture
concepts.body: AWS Network Firewall is implemented by creating firewall endpoints in dedicated subnets within a VPC (one endpoint per Availability Zone you want protected), and then modifying route tables so that traffic that should be inspected is routed through these firewall subnet endpoints rather than going directly to its destination. Getting the subnet and route table layout right, a distinct firewall subnet separate from public and private application subnets, is the first and most error-prone implementation step, since AWS requires specific routing patterns for the firewall to sit correctly in-line.

concepts.heading: Building Firewall Policies from Rule Groups
concepts.body: A firewall policy is composed of one or more rule groups, which come in stateless (evaluated first, extremely fast pass/drop/forward decisions based on simple 5-tuple matches) and stateful (connection-aware, supporting more expressive 5-tuple rules, domain-based rules, and Suricata-compatible IDS/IPS signature rules) varieties, and implementation requires deciding the default stateless action plus which stateful rule groups apply and in what order/priority.

concepts.heading: Domain-Based Filtering Implementation
concepts.body: Domain list rule groups let you allow or deny outbound traffic based on domain names, such as blocking known malicious domains or restricting egress to only approved SaaS domains, and because Network Firewall inspects the TLS Server Name Indication (SNI) field, this filtering works even though the actual payload remains encrypted, without requiring TLS termination. Implementers should note that domain filtering by SNI only sees the hostname the client requests, not the full URL, so path-based filtering is not possible at this layer.

concepts.heading: Deploying Centralized Inspection at Scale
concepts.body: For an organization-wide deployment, Network Firewall is typically implemented once in a centralized inspection VPC rather than duplicated in every spoke VPC, both to reduce operational overhead and to guarantee a single, consistent point of policy enforcement for all traffic. AWS Firewall Manager then layers on top to push a standard Network Firewall policy automatically to every VPC (existing and newly created) across an AWS Organization, removing the need to manually attach the firewall to each new account or VPC as it's created.

concepts.heading: Logging and Alerting for Firewall Decisions
concepts.body: Network Firewall logging configuration should be implemented alongside the firewall itself, sending alert logs and flow logs to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Amazon Data Firehose, since without this configured explicitly, no logs are generated by default. These logs are the primary evidence used to tune rule groups over time, for example confirming a new domain-block rule is actually catching the intended traffic before switching its action from alert to drop.

examPoints: Blocking outbound traffic to specific malicious domains, even when the traffic is encrypted (HTTPS), points to Network Firewall's domain-based rule groups using TLS SNI inspection, not IP-based rules.

Automatically deploying a consistent Network Firewall policy to every current and future VPC across an AWS Organization is implemented with AWS Firewall Manager, not by manually configuring Network Firewall in each account.

quiz.q: A security team must block outbound connections to a list of known-malicious domains, even for HTTPS traffic where the payload is encrypted. Which Network Firewall capability enables this?
choices: Stateful domain-list rules using TLS SNI inspection
quiz.explain: Domain-list rule groups inspect the TLS SNI field to identify the requested domain even when the payload itself is encrypted; stateless 5-tuple rules cannot match on domain names.

quiz.q: An organization wants a consistent Network Firewall policy automatically applied to every VPC, including ones created in the future, across its entire AWS Organization. What should they use?
choices: Manually attach Network Firewall to each new VPC
AWS Firewall Manager with an organization-wide Network Firewall policy
quiz.explain: Firewall Manager centrally manages and automatically applies security policies, including Network Firewall, across all accounts and VPCs (present and future) in an Organization.

days.recap: Implementing Network Firewall means placing firewall endpoints correctly and routing traffic through them, layering stateless and stateful rule groups (including domain filtering via TLS SNI), centralizing deployment in an inspection VPC, using Firewall Manager for organization-wide consistency, and explicitly enabling logging to support ongoing rule tuning.

days.title: Implementing Complex Hybrid and Multi-Account DNS

concepts.heading: Implementing Conditional Forwarding Rules
concepts.body: Conditional forwarding is implemented in Route 53 Resolver as a forwarding rule scoped to a specific domain (for example corp.internal), which sends only queries matching that domain out through the outbound Resolver endpoint to specified on-premises DNS server IP addresses, while all other queries continue to be resolved normally by Route 53. Getting the rule's domain scope precise matters: an overly broad domain would send all queries on-premises, while an overly narrow one would fail to catch subdomains that also need forwarding, unless a separate rule is added for those.

concepts.heading: Implementing Layered Traffic Management Policies
concepts.body: Complex traffic management, such as sending 90% of traffic to a new application version in one Region while distributing the remaining 10% across other Regions by latency, is implemented by nesting Route 53 routing policies inside a Traffic Flow policy record: a weighted policy for the canary split, feeding into latency-based policies for regional distribution, all authored visually and saved as a single versioned traffic policy that can be quickly rolled back if needed. Implementers should version each meaningful change so a bad configuration can be reverted instantly.

concepts.heading: Enabling DNSSEC on a Hosted Zone
concepts.body: Enabling DNSSEC signing on a public hosted zone requires creating a Key Signing Key (KSK), which can be managed by Route 53 itself or by an external key stored in AWS CloudHSM for stricter key custody requirements, and then establishing a chain of trust by creating a corresponding DS (Delegation Signer) record at the parent zone or domain registrar. If the DS record at the registrar does not correctly match the KSK, resolvers that perform DNSSEC validation will fail to resolve the domain entirely, unlike many other configuration mistakes that merely degrade rather than break resolution.

concepts.heading: Sharing Resolver Rules Across Accounts with AWS RAM
concepts.body: Rather than recreating the same conditional forwarding rules in every AWS account that needs to reach an on-premises DNS server, the resolver rules are created once in a central network account and shared to other accounts (or an entire Organization) using AWS RAM, after which each recipient account associates the shared rule with its own VPCs to activate the forwarding behavior locally. This keeps forwarding logic centrally maintained while still requiring each consuming account to explicitly associate the rule with the VPCs that need it.

concepts.heading: Troubleshooting Complex DNS Implementations
concepts.body: When hybrid DNS resolution doesn't behave as expected, a systematic check includes confirming the forwarding rule's domain scope actually matches the query name, verifying the resolver rule is associated with the correct VPC, confirming security groups on the Resolver endpoint ENIs allow DNS (UDP/TCP 53) from the expected sources, and checking whether a more specific private hosted zone is unexpectedly intercepting queries before they reach the forwarding rule.

examPoints: When only queries for a specific domain (such as corp.internal) should be sent to an on-premises DNS server, and all other queries should still resolve normally through Route 53, the implementation is a Resolver conditional forwarding rule scoped to that domain, not a blanket forward of all traffic.

An incorrectly configured DS record at the domain registrar after enabling DNSSEC will cause total resolution failure for validating resolvers, making DS record accuracy a critical implementation checkpoint, not just a best practice.

quiz.q: A company wants queries only for the domain corp.internal to be forwarded to an on-premises DNS server, while all other queries continue to resolve through Route 53 normally. What should they implement?
choices: Forward all DNS queries to on-premises
A Route 53 Resolver conditional forwarding rule scoped to corp.internal
A public hosted zone for corp.internal
quiz.explain: A domain-scoped forwarding rule sends only matching queries on-premises while leaving all other resolution behavior unchanged; forwarding all queries would break resolution for everything else.

quiz.q: After enabling DNSSEC on a public hosted zone, external resolvers that validate DNSSEC suddenly fail to resolve the domain at all. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The DS record at the domain registrar does not match the zone's Key Signing Key
Too many A records exist in the zone
A CNAME record was used at the zone apex
quiz.explain: An incorrect or missing DS record breaks the DNSSEC chain of trust, causing validating resolvers to treat the zone as unresolvable, unlike most misconfigurations which only degrade performance.

days.recap: Complex hybrid DNS implementation combines domain-scoped conditional forwarding rules, layered Traffic Flow routing policies, careful DNSSEC key and DS record setup, and AWS RAM sharing of Resolver rules so forwarding logic stays centrally managed but explicitly opted into per VPC.

days.title: Sharing Network Resources with AWS Resource Access Manager

concepts.heading: How AWS RAM Sharing Works
concepts.body: AWS Resource Access Manager lets a resource-owning account share specific resources, including Transit Gateways, Route 53 Resolver rules, and subnets (for VPC Sharing), directly with other AWS accounts or Organizational Units, without duplicating or recreating the resource in each account. Sharing is initiated by the owning account, and the receiving account must accept the invitation unless sharing is done within an AWS Organization with the necessary trust enabled, in which case acceptance can be automatic.

concepts.heading: Ownership, Access, and Billing Model
concepts.body: Once a resource is shared and accepted, the recipient account can use it largely as if it were their own, for example attaching a VPC to a shared Transit Gateway, but the resource's ownership and most billing remain with the originating account. VPC Sharing is a deliberate exception worth remembering: subnets are shared, but resources launched into those subnets by participant accounts are billed to the participant account that created them, not to the VPC-owning account.

concepts.heading: Automatic Sharing Across an Organization
concepts.body: When AWS RAM sharing is configured with AWS Organizations integration, resources can be shared with an entire Organizational Unit rather than individual account IDs, and this extends automatically to any new account added to that OU in the future, with no manual re-sharing step required. This is the standard mechanism ensuring new business units gain access to shared infrastructure like a central Transit Gateway immediately, without waiting on a manual sharing action.

concepts.heading: Access Control and Unsharing Considerations
concepts.body: AWS RAM's sharing action itself does not replace fine-grained IAM permissions; a recipient account still needs appropriate IAM permissions to act on the shared resource, so RAM sharing and IAM policy are complementary layers, not substitutes. Before unsharing a resource, check for dependent resources in recipient accounts, since removing a share can break connectivity in ways that are not always immediately obvious from the owning account's perspective.

examPoints: A requirement for a centrally managed Transit Gateway or Resolver rule to be usable by many accounts without rebuilding it per account is a direct signal for AWS RAM sharing.

A requirement that new accounts added to a specific Organizational Unit automatically gain access to shared network resources, with no manual step, points to RAM sharing configured with AWS Organizations integration.

quiz.q: A company wants a centrally managed Transit Gateway to be usable by dozens of AWS accounts without recreating it in each one. What should they use?
choices: Create a duplicate Transit Gateway per account
Share the Transit Gateway using AWS Resource Access Manager
Use VPC Peering between all accounts
Manually export and import Transit Gateway configuration
quiz.explain: AWS RAM allows a single Transit Gateway to be shared and attached to VPCs across many accounts without duplication.

quiz.q: A company wants any new AWS account added to its 'Workloads' Organizational Unit to automatically gain access to a shared Route 53 Resolver rule with no manual action. What should they configure?
choices: Manually re-share the rule with each new account as it is created
RAM sharing targeted at the Organizational Unit, integrated with AWS Organizations
A separate Resolver rule per account
IAM policies alone, without RAM sharing
quiz.explain: Sharing a resource with an Organizational Unit via RAM's AWS Organizations integration automatically extends access to new accounts joining that OU.

days.recap: AWS RAM shares resources like Transit Gateways and Resolver rules across accounts without duplication, keeping ownership and most billing with the originating account (except VPC Sharing's subnet resources), and integrating with AWS Organizations lets sharing automatically extend to new accounts in a target OU.

days.title: Automating Network Infrastructure

concepts.heading: Infrastructure as Code for Repeatable Networking
concepts.body: Defining VPCs, subnets, route tables, and Transit Gateway attachments in CloudFormation or the AWS CDK turns network configuration into version-controlled, repeatable code that can be deployed identically across development, staging, and production accounts, eliminating configuration drift from manually clicking through the console. CDK in particular allows higher-level abstractions (constructs) that encapsulate networking best practices, such as a reusable 'standard VPC' construct, reducing the chance of a manual mistake being repeated across environments.

concepts.heading: Event-Driven Network Automation
concepts.body: Amazon EventBridge can capture network-related events, such as a VPN tunnel transitioning to a DOWN state, a Transit Gateway attachment state change, or a Direct Connect connection state change, and route them to targets like Lambda functions or SNS topics to trigger automated notification or remediation. This event-driven pattern reduces the mean time to detect network failures compared to relying solely on periodic polling or manual dashboard checks.

concepts.heading: Modularizing IaC for Reuse
concepts.body: As network IaC grows, breaking configuration into nested stacks or CDK constructs for standard, reusable components, parameterized for environment-specific values (CIDR ranges, Availability Zones, tags), lets teams stamp out consistent network foundations quickly while still allowing controlled per-environment customization. This modular approach also makes it far easier to apply a security or compliance fix once, in the shared module, and have it propagate to every environment on the next deployment.

concepts.heading: Filling Gaps with CLI and SDK Automation
concepts.body: Some networking automation needs, particularly dynamic scenarios like allocating the next available CIDR block from a centrally tracked IP address pool at deployment time, are awkward to express in declarative IaC templates and are better handled with AWS CLI scripts or SDK-based custom logic, sometimes wrapped as a CloudFormation custom resource so it still participates in a stack's lifecycle. Recognizing when a requirement calls for this kind of imperative, runtime-computed logic versus pure declarative IaC is a practical implementation skill.

examPoints: A requirement to detect a VPN tunnel going down and automatically trigger a notification or remediation action is implemented with EventBridge routing the state-change event to a Lambda function or SNS topic, not periodic manual checks.

A requirement to deploy identical, repeatable network configurations across dev/staging/production points to CloudFormation or CDK-based Infrastructure as Code, not manual console configuration per environment.

quiz.q: A network team wants to be automatically notified within seconds whenever a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel transitions to a DOWN state, without polling. What should they implement?
choices: A scheduled Lambda function that checks tunnel status every hour
An EventBridge rule matching the VPN state-change event, targeting an SNS topic or Lambda function
Manual review of the VPN console each morning
quiz.explain: EventBridge can react to VPN tunnel state-change events in near real time and trigger automated notification or remediation, unlike periodic polling which introduces detection delay.

quiz.q: A team needs to deploy an identical VPC and subnet layout consistently across dev, staging, and production accounts, avoiding manual console drift. What approach best satisfies this?
choices: Manually configure each environment via the console
Define the network as a reusable CloudFormation or CDK template/construct, parameterized per environment
Use only CLI one-off commands each time
Copy screenshots of the console configuration as documentation
quiz.explain: Infrastructure as Code with parameterization ensures consistent, repeatable deployments across environments and avoids the drift inherent in manual console configuration.

days.recap: Automating network infrastructure combines CloudFormation/CDK for repeatable, version-controlled deployments, EventBridge-driven automation for reacting to network state changes, modular reusable IaC components for consistency at scale, and CLI/SDK scripting for dynamic scenarios that don't fit cleanly into declarative templates.

days.title: Domain 2 Review: Network Implementation

concepts.heading: From Design to Working Configuration
concepts.body: This week translated Domain 1's design decisions into concrete implementation steps: choosing the correct virtual interface type and verifying BGP state, building segmented Transit Gateway route tables and inspection VPC routing, configuring Network Firewall policies and domain filtering, and setting up conditional DNS forwarding and DNSSEC. The throughline is that implementation success is measured by specific, checkable states, BGP Established, correct route table associations, firewall logs showing expected matches, DS records matching KSKs, rather than a vague sense that 'the connection works'.

concepts.heading: Segmentation and Inspection as Implementation Patterns
concepts.body: The multiple-route-table segmentation pattern and the inspection VPC pattern are two of the most reusable implementation templates across the exam, appearing in slightly different guises whenever a scenario asks you to isolate certain traffic or force it through a checkpoint. Being able to sketch, from memory, the route table entries needed on both the spoke and hub/inspection sides for each pattern is a strong indicator of readiness for this domain.

concepts.heading: Sharing and Automation as Force Multipliers
concepts.body: AWS RAM sharing and Infrastructure-as-Code automation both solve the same underlying problem at different layers, avoiding duplicated, drifting configuration across many accounts and environments, and questions about 'a large organization with many accounts needing consistent X' should trigger you to consider both RAM sharing (for actual AWS resources) and IaC (for configuration templates) as complementary answers.

concepts.heading: Implementation Domain Exam Strategy
concepts.body: Network Implementation carries 26% of the exam weight, second only to Design, and tends to test specific configuration details (which VIF type, which route table needs which entry, which RAM sharing behavior) rather than high-level architecture choices, so review by testing yourself on exact mechanics rather than just service names.

examPoints: When reviewing, for each service this week ask yourself 'what is the specific state or setting I would check to confirm this was implemented correctly', not just 'what does this service do'.
Segmentation (multiple route tables) and centralized inspection (inspection VPC pattern) are reusable templates; practice sketching the exact route entries for both from memory.

quiz.q: Which Direct Connect virtual interface type is required specifically to connect to a Transit Gateway?
quiz.explain: A transit VIF is the specific interface type required to connect Direct Connect to a Transit Gateway, distinguishing it from a private VIF used for direct VPC connections.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to force all outbound internet traffic from multiple spoke VPCs through a centralized AWS Network Firewall?
choices: Deploy Network Firewall independently in each spoke VPC
Implement the inspection VPC pattern with Transit Gateway route tables directing spoke traffic through a central firewall VPC
quiz.explain: The inspection VPC pattern with correctly configured Transit Gateway and VPC route tables is the standard implementation for centralized traffic inspection across multiple spokes.

days.recap: Domain 2 review reinforces that implementation is verified through specific checkable states (BGP Established, correct route associations, firewall log matches, valid DS records), with segmentation and inspection VPC patterns, RAM sharing, and Infrastructure as Code as the recurring reusable techniques worth 26% of the exam.

days.title: Maintaining Routing and Connectivity

concepts.heading: Monitoring BGP Session Health Over Time
concepts.body: Ongoing operations require continuously monitoring BGP session state (Established, Idle, Active, Connect) rather than only checking it once at implementation time, since a session can flap due to underlying physical link instability, and frequent flapping degrades routing stability even if the session is Established at any given check. CloudWatch metrics for Direct Connect virtual interfaces and VPN tunnels expose BGP session state changes and can be alarmed on, so operations teams are notified of instability rather than discovering it only when application-level symptoms appear.

concepts.heading: Accelerating Failure Detection with BFD
concepts.body: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is a lightweight protocol that runs alongside BGP to detect link or forwarding-path failures in milliseconds, far faster than BGP's own hold-timer-based detection, and enabling BFD on Direct Connect virtual interfaces significantly reduces failover time in active-passive or active-active redundant designs. BFD needs to be supported and configured on both the AWS side and the customer router, and mismatched BFD configuration between the two sides can itself become a source of session instability.

concepts.heading: Handling Planned Direct Connect Maintenance
concepts.body: AWS periodically schedules planned maintenance on Direct Connect infrastructure and publishes these events through the AWS Health Dashboard, giving operations teams advance notice to proactively shift traffic to a redundant path before the maintenance window begins, rather than experiencing an unplanned-feeling outage. Subscribing to AWS Health events programmatically via EventBridge allows automated pre-maintenance traffic shifting rather than relying on someone manually reading dashboard notifications.

concepts.heading: VPN Tunnel Health and Dead Peer Detection
concepts.body: Site-to-Site VPN tunnel health should be monitored via CloudWatch metrics such as TunnelState, and Dead Peer Detection (DPD) configuration determines how quickly a tunnel recognizes that its peer has become unresponsive and tears down the stale session so failover can occur; a DPD timeout set too high delays failover unnecessarily, while one set too low can cause unnecessary flapping over transient network blips. Reviewing DPD and BGP hold-timer settings periodically, especially after any change to the on-premises network path, is a routine operational task.

concepts.heading: Operational Runbooks for Connectivity Incidents
concepts.body: Mature operations maintain a documented runbook for hybrid connectivity incidents that specifies, in order, which dashboards and metrics to check first, how to manually force a failover if automatic failover doesn't trigger as expected, and clear escalation paths, since ad hoc troubleshooting during an actual outage is slower and more error-prone than following a rehearsed procedure. Regularly testing failover in a controlled maintenance window validates that the redundancy design and runbook actually work as intended.

examPoints: A requirement to detect a link failure and trigger BGP re-convergence in milliseconds rather than tens of seconds points to enabling BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) alongside BGP.

Advance notice of planned Direct Connect maintenance, allowing proactive traffic shifting before an outage window, is delivered through the AWS Health Dashboard, which can also be consumed programmatically via EventBridge.

quiz.q: A company needs BGP to detect a failed Direct Connect link and fail over to a backup path within milliseconds, rather than waiting for standard BGP hold timers to expire. What should they enable?
quiz.explain: BFD detects forwarding-path failures far faster than BGP's own timers, dramatically speeding up failover; the other options are unrelated to failure detection speed.

quiz.q: Where can a network operations team find advance notice of AWS-scheduled Direct Connect maintenance events to proactively shift traffic beforehand?
quiz.explain: The AWS Health Dashboard publishes account-specific events including scheduled Direct Connect maintenance, which can also be consumed via EventBridge for automation.
